html:
In 1257 the volcano Samalas on the Indonesian island of Lombok blew apart in one of the largest eruptions of the last several thousand years. It left a caldera that now holds the lake Segara Anak, beside Mount Rinjani.

Ice cores from both Greenland and Antarctica had long shown a huge burst of sulphur in the middle 1200s from an unknown volcano. In 2013 scientists matched it to Samalas, using dated ash, the shape of the caldera and palm leaf chronicles, the Babad Lombok, which tell of a mountain collapsing and burying the royal town of Pamatan.

The sulphur cooled the world's climate for a few years. Chronicles in Europe report a cold, wet year in 1258 with failed harvests and famine, though how much of that came from Samalas is debated. Some scholars see it as one of the eruptions that helped start the Little Ice Age. Compare the volcanic winter of 536 and the 1815 Tambora eruption on the next island east.
